cells.tense: You're steering by a light you recognize, and the direction holds without you forcing it.
cells.ask: Write down the one direction you keep circling back to. Put it where you'll see it, then take a single step that faces it this week.
cells.core:
The pull toward what you want is steady and you're not arguing with it. The next step is close enough that taking it doesn't cost much: you move, you adjust, you move again. Nothing is grinding at you.

What keeps it that way is that you keep going. The pull doesn't need your protection — it needs your feet. Keep taking the plain step in front of you, the one that faces the direction rather than proving it. And let some of the strength you spend holding things for other people land back on you too. You can stand under your own direction and let it carry its own weight.

cells.verb: steering by the light you recognize
cells.place: where the pull toward what you actually want lives

cells.tense: You'll be steering by a light you haven't reached yet, and you're already bracing for the turn.
cells.ask: Before you act on it, say the direction out loud to one person and stop. Listen to what comes back before you decide again.
cells.core:
You're designing what comes next before you've walked the ground you're on. What it'll do, what it'll show, what it'll mean — sorted and settled ahead of time. Setting a direction is fine. Defending one that hasn't arrived yet is where the tightness lives, and the real pull doesn't need all the arrangements.

Most of what you've planned won't happen the way you planned it. The thing you're drawn to will still be there tomorrow whether or not you've finished working it out tonight. Get one other person's read on it and let that be real. The direction survives being seen by someone else; what doesn't survive is keeping it all in your own head.

cells.tense: You're standing at a doorway you've already walked through, and the pull isn't moving you.
cells.ask: Pick one direction you used to feel clear about. Talk about it with someone you trust, and let the conversation go where it goes.
cells.core:
You have a pull toward something and you're not letting it move you. The waiting has become the place you live — waiting for the light to prove itself before you budge an inch. The pull hasn't gone anywhere. The walking stopped.

Getting moving again doesn't take a big decision. It takes small and it takes someone else: say what you're drawn to out loud, without defending it, and let a person hear it. Then look at one thing that's gone well lately and set it next to the direction. Those two belong in the same room. Let them talk, and let the larger one pull.
cells.sheetLine: The pull is still there. You just haven't let it move you.

cells.tense: You're steering by your own light right now and calling it something else — the situation, not a choice.
cells.ask: Name one decision you're treating as automatic. Say plainly that it was chosen, then let someone else carry one of its loads.
cells.core:
The direction you're living has your name on it. You've been describing it as the situation, the family's expectation, the only sensible path — a neutral report rather than a call you made. The steering is real and it's working, and you're doing it without standing behind it in your own mind.

You don't have to announce anything or defend the choice. Say it once, plainly, and let the day keep going. Then let one person carry something that's on your list, without you fixing it for them first. The direction sits better when there's a person in it instead of a set of conditions, and you're the person already doing the steering.
